explanation:
## How the puzzle works

**What the grid contains.** Each input holds one small figure, sometimes with a stray single cell nearby. In pair 1 that stray cell is the lone 3 at (3,1). In pair 2 it is the lone 4 at (7,6), and in pair 3 it is the lone 9 at (2,6). The output never deletes anything. It only adds cells, and the added cells always copy colours already present in the figure.

**What gets added.** Look at pair 3. The 8-block is a 3×3 square, and there is a single 9 at its top-right diagonal corner. In the output, 9s appear at all four diagonal corners. Every output is therefore the input together with its copies rotated by 90°, 180° and 270° about a centre point.

**Where the centre is.** The centre is not always the centre of the bounding box. In pair 1 the stray 3 changes the box. So I made the inspect search over every possible centre, in half-cell steps. A centre is valid only if two conditions hold:
- every rotated cell lands inside the grid on an integer cell;
- no rotated cell lands on a cell that already has a *different* colour.

Among the valid centres, the program chooses the one that adds the fewest new cells. That is the centre where the input already "almost" has 4-fold symmetry. In doubled coordinates the centres found were (9,5), (10,8) and (8,8), which are (4.5, 2.5), (5,4) and (4,4) in real cells. With those centres, all three train outputs were reproduced exactly.

**Test input.** The best centre is (4,4), which is the centre cell holding colour 3. Rotating the 3/2 pattern around it fills in a cross-shaped figure with 4-fold symmetry. For example, the 2 stub at (2,4) becomes 2s at (4,2), (6,4) and (4,6), and the arms of 3s get mirrored onto the right side and above/below.

**Construction stages.** I start from the input. Then I stamp the 90° copy, the 180° copy and the 270° copy one after another, emitting the canvas after each stamp. The last emit is the final answer.
